Both failed with exactly the values the proposal reported — skipping occurrence[2] moved next_date from 2017-01-02 to 2017-01-09, and posting today with date=occurrence[2] stamped schedule_occurrence 2017-01-02 instead of 2017-01-16. I also ran the baseline the change starts from: src/server/schedules/app.test.ts, 48 tests green. Every structural claim I checked held — the two dropped `date`s in Account.tsx's switch, `occurrence = today ? schedule.next_date : ...` at app.ts:570 with its `if (!today)` guard, skipNextDate as a bare `setNextDate({id, advance: true})`, `reset` being only a column-selection branch with the sole arithmetic switch at app.ts:239-241, the bare `setNextDate({id})` at :796 taking that same path, all four mobile onSkip handlers hand-parsing while their onPost siblings already send `date`, the single unpaidDates filter, and the two today-semantics tests at :1387 and :1512. I confirmed the v1 forecast objection is a real hole: normalizeSchedule does rebuild the record field by field, getFutureOccurrenceDates seeds from next_date and pushes every occurrence, and buildFutureScheduleOccurrences filters only on isScheduleOccurrencePosted. I also swept further than the proposal did and resolved one of its four unknowns favorably — schedules_next_date has exactly two writers (setNextDate's db.update at :254 and one insertWithUUID at :344), so no caller reconstructs the row wholesale and the new column cannot be silently dropped. What holds this at 82: the fix is entirely unwritten, so the bounded loop in setNextDate and the new f('json') plus view-override plumbing are design-until-executed, and the loop nests inside getNextDateAfter's own MAX_ADVANCE_ATTEMPTS loop, so the worst case is multiplicative rather than 7 steps. Two things remain untraced: how packages/crdt merges concurrent writes to a new column on schedules_next_date, and whether any VRT snapshot covers register Upcoming rows. Neither fails silently in the dangerous direction.
work_order.understanding: Two menu actions on an Upcoming preview row name one occurrence and act on another, and I have now watched both happen rather than infer it. onScheduleAction (Account.tsx:1558-1594) parses every preview id into {scheduleId, date} via parsePreviewId and then drops date on exactly the post-transaction-today and skip branches. Server-side, postTransactionForSchedule (app.ts:570) computes `const occurrence = today ? schedule.next_date : (date ?? schedule.next_date)` with an `if (!today)` duplicate guard, so today discharges the schedule's head whatever the caller named, and skipNextDate (app.ts:466-467) is `setNextDate({ id, advance: true })`, which advances the head one step past whatever row was clicked. My own run against unmodified code: skipping occurrence[2] moved next_date from 2017-01-02 to 2017-01-09, taking two occurrences the user was still owed with it; posting today with date=occurrence[2] stamped schedule_occurrence 2017-01-02 rather than 2017-01-16. The two branches are one defect in one switch but not the same amount of work. Posting already has a per-occurrence record — the schedule_occurrence stamp, which computeSchedulePreviewTransactions already filters on — so threading date is sufficient. Skipping writes no transaction, so nothing anywhere records that the chosen occurrence will not happen: next_date is a single anchor and every occurrence before it has already fallen off. Threading the date is necessary but not sufficient for skip; the handler needs somewhere to write the occurrence down, and every reader of occurrence dates has to learn to honour it — including the forecast, which is the read site v1 missed and would otherwise have traded a wrong register for a wrong balance projection.
work_order.root_cause: onScheduleAction discards the occurrence it just parsed on the post-transaction-today and skip branches, and both server handlers predate the occurrence being part of the request: postTransactionForSchedule hard-codes schedule.next_date as the discharged occurrence whenever `today` is set, and skipNextDate has no occurrence parameter at all. The transport already carries it — the post-transaction branch and all four mobile onPost handlers already send date. The handlers do not read it.
work_order.approach:
Thread the parsed occurrence date through both handlers, and give the skip half a record the rest of the app can read.

Posting: post-transaction-today sends {id, date, today: true}; `const occurrence = date ?? schedule.next_date` for both paths, with `today` still deciding the transaction's own date and no longer the discharged occurrence. Callers that name no occurrence (the Schedules page sends {id, today: true}; advanceSchedulesService sends {id}) resolve date to undefined and are unchanged. The duplicate guard widens to `if (!today || date != null)`.

Skipping: a nullable `skipped_occurrences` TEXT column on schedules_next_date (additive migration, id a current timestamp sorting after 1790969762045), exposed as `f('json')` on the schedules schema and `_nd.skipped_occurrences` in the v_schedules view — both required, because views.ts:26-29 spreads the table's public fields then the view's overrides, so a schema entry alone would emit `_.skipped_occurrences` against a column the schedules table does not have. skipNextDate({id, date}) keeps today's advance when date is absent or equals next_date (keeping IAC-3 true) and otherwise records the occurrence, deduped, sorted, entries at or before next_date dropped.

The skip-stepping loop wraps the newNextDate computation in setNextDate unconditionally — not into an advance or reset branch. `reset` is not an arithmetic branch; it only chooses which columns the db.update writes. The sole arithmetic switch is `advance ? getNextDateAfter(...) : getNextDate(...)` at app.ts:239-241, and the bare setNextDate({id}) at :796 takes that same path, so a loop written only into the advance branch would silently miss the path that could auto-post a skipped occurrence. Bound it with the existing MAX_ADVANCE_ATTEMPTS, never replacing the getNextDateAfter call. Consume and prune skipped entries in the same db.update.

The user-visible symptom quoted in the issue body is QA's report on the epic, which is data. The reproduction above is mine: I wrote both cases against unmodified production code and watched them fail.

alternatives_considered.approach: Make the preview's `status === 'paid'` shift account for which occurrence was actually paid (the issue's second offered shape).
alternatives_considered.rejected_because: The shift exists to hide the head occurrence the stamp filter cannot see, because getHasTransactionsQuery only ever asks about next_date. Teaching it about occurrences duplicates a concept the preview already models one filter below it, and it fixes nothing for skip: with no transaction written there is no paid occurrence to shift for, and next_date would still have moved while the chosen row stayed listed.

alternatives_considered.approach: Record the skip as a transaction row carrying the schedule link and an occurrence stamp (a zero-amount hidden row standing in for 'consumed without a payment').
alternatives_considered.rejected_because: It fabricates a transaction the user never made and lies to everything downstream: getHasTransactionsQuery would answer 'paid', hasTransactionForSchedule and advanceSchedulesService would treat it as a payment, and it would surface in exports. The tombstoned variant is worse — executors.ts appends `tombstone = 0` to every live query, so it would be invisible to the queries that need to read it.

alternatives_considered.approach: Store the skip as an `exdate` exception on the schedule's date condition in the rule, which every occurrence computation already funnels through recurConfigToRSchedule.
alternatives_considered.rejected_because: The date condition is also the rule that MATCHES transactions: a Condition('is'|'isapprox','date',value) builds its RSchedule from that value, so excepting a date silently stops an imported or rule-created transaction on that date from being linked to its schedule — a far wider behavioural change than this bug. It also round-trips badly: ScheduleEditModal rebuilds the value as {start, frequency, patterns} from form fields, so every schedule edit would silently drop the skips.

alternatives_considered.approach: Hide 'Skip next scheduled date' on rows that are not next_date, the way #59 hides it on one-off schedules.
alternatives_considered.rejected_because: It makes the wrong behaviour unreachable instead of correct and fails IAC-1 outright: the criterion requires the chosen row to leave the register while the earlier ones stay.

alternatives_considered.approach: Advance next_date to the occurrence after the one that was clicked, so the skipped date falls off the end of the window.
alternatives_considered.rejected_because: That is the current bug with an extra step, and my reproduction shows exactly what it costs: on a later row next_date went 2017-01-02 → 2017-01-09, taking occurrences the user was owed with it. Advancing further would take more.

alternatives_considered.approach: Put skipped_occurrences on the `schedules` table rather than on schedules_next_date, leaving the next-date row untouched entirely.
alternatives_considered.rejected_because: schedules_next_date is the row that already owns the schedule's mutable date state, is the only other thing setNextDate writes, and already syncs; schedules is joined to it only through the v_schedules view. Putting the column on schedules would mean a second write path to a table otherwise updated wholesale by insertWithSchema/updateWithSchema, and it would not sit beside the next_date the loop has to consult in the same db.update.

alternatives_considered.approach: Leave the forecast out of scope as v1 did, and record the behaviour change as a residual risk.
alternatives_considered.rejected_because: The v1 review was right that this is not a risk to record but a defect the change would introduce: before, skipping moved next_date forward so the forecast dropped the date as a side effect; after, next_date deliberately stays put and the skip lives in a column the forecast never reads, so the forecast keeps counting money the user explicitly said they are not paying. Trading a wrong register for a wrong balance projection is not a smaller bug. I confirmed it by reading forecast-schedules.ts; the cost of covering it is one type field, one return field and one `continue`.

alternatives_considered.approach: Split the issue: land the posting half (small, low risk) and file the skip half separately, since it needs a migration.
alternatives_considered.rejected_because: The issue states both branches are one defect in one switch and both IACs are on the ticket. Shipping only the posting half leaves Skip next scheduled date silently consuming an occurrence the user never named — the higher-severity of the two, since it drops money rather than mis-dating it.

This invariant is what makes it safe for skip to be additive rather than something posting has to check — and it is load-bearing, which is why AC-9 tests it through all three setNextDate call shapes.

work_order.debate_summary:
There was no critique to judge this round — plan/critique.json is an empty object, the critic wrote nothing. So the only adversarial artefact I had was the brief's rejection of v1, and against that the proposal is a straight answer rather than a debate: both required items were done rather than argued. What I did instead was verify, independently, on the theory that an unopposed plan deserves more scrutiny rather than less.

I reproduced the defect myself. I wrote the two cases from scratch as a scratch test file against unmodified production code and ran them: both failed, with exactly the values the proposal reported (next_date 2017-01-09 instead of 2017-01-02; schedule_occurrence 2017-01-02 instead of 2017-01-16). That matters more than agreement would have: the diagnosis, the reproduction and the work order are three independent arrivals at the same fact, and the two failing cases become real regression tests rather than assertions written to match an implementation. I also ran the baseline the change starts from (app.test.ts, 48 green) and swept the callers, the AQL plumbing, the migration rule, the four mobile handlers and the two tests this change deliberately overturns. Every structural claim held.

The v1 forecast objection was the substantive one and the proposal is right to have taken it as a hole rather than a wording slip. I confirmed it independently: normalizeSchedule rebuilds the record field by field, so a new column is dropped even though the query is select('*'), and buildFutureScheduleOccurrences filters only on isScheduleOccurrencePosted. Left uncovered, this change would have traded a wrong register for a wrong balance projection. I kept the fix and gave it AC-10, its own test file and its own QA step, because a filter that silently reads an empty array fails with no visible symptom.

Three things I changed rather than accepted. First, the migration: the proposal names a literal id, 1791500000000, which is dated four days in the future. Sorted it would work, but a work order that names a literal filename invites that filename being typed, and a future-dated id sorts after migrations that land before it. The work order now says take a current timestamp at write time and re-check the directory. Second, I swept further than the proposal did and resolved one of its four open unknowns in its favour: schedules_next_date has exactly two writers and no wholesale reconstruction anywhere, including schedule.edit, so the new column cannot be silently dropped by an edit path. Third, in each of the four mobile files there is a second hand-rolled split('/') in the onComplete handler directly below the onSkip one; the work order says explicitly not to convert that one, because complete names no occurrence.

What I rejected outright is the proposal's route_request. It asked for needs_earlier_stage at stage qa, on the reasoning that the plan's defining claim flipped from reproduced:false to true. QA is already on this ticket's route (plan → implement → review → qa) and QA is not an earlier stage than plan — the request is incoherent as written, and the pipeline would have been asked to act on a stage that is already present. I dropped it and recorded no route_request. The route itself is right for this work: it touches money and date arithmetic and a synced-table migration, and it carries both review and QA, which is what a change like this needs.

I did not re-plan the substance, and I want to be plain that I did not test the fix — it does not exist yet. Everything above is a verified diagnosis plus a design checked against the code it will land in; the loop, the JSON plumbing and the migration are unexecuted. The honest limit on this score is that shape, not doubt about the diagnosis, and it is why I sit at 82 rather than the 84 the proposal claimed for itself.
residual_risks: The setNextDate loop is the highest-consequence piece and nothing has watched it run — I reproduced the defect, not the fix. If it is written with the wrong bound, or unbounded against a schedule whose every future occurrence is recorded as skipped, it can spin; and it nests inside getNextDateAfter's own 7-attempt loop, so the worst case is multiplicative. MAX_ADVANCE_ATTEMPTS is the bound to reuse; a reviewer should read that loop first.

The forecast filter is the newly added piece and it fails silently by design: it omits rather than errors. It has AC-10, a dedicated test file and a QA step that watches the projected balance, but the why belongs in a code comment there and not only in the PR description.

There is no way to un-skip an occurrence. Once recorded it hides that date until next_date has moved past it and the prune drops it, which for a long-running schedule may be months. Deliberate — undo is out of scope — but worth saying in the PR description rather than discovering in QA.

The skip list is pruned only on the next setNextDate write, so a schedule that is skipped repeatedly and never advances keeps growing the array. Bounded by the number of occurrences a user chooses to skip rather than by anything exponential, but nothing enforces a ceiling.

Cross-version sync: an older client writing schedules_next_date drops a recorded skip, and a newer client will hide that occurrence from a client that never skipped it. Same class of exposure schedule_occurrence already carries, and the failure direction is 'an occurrence shows again', never 'a payment is lost'.

QA step 11 deliberately reloads the page to prove the skip is persisted rather than filtered in memory. If that step is skipped, the change could pass QA while the column write is silently absent — the persisted record is the one part no purely visual check can see.

Because the critic produced nothing again this round, there is still no adversarial reading of this plan from another agent. I verified the reproduction, the plumbing and the callers myself and found the diagnosis sound, but the class of defect that survives that is the one that only shows when the code runs — which is the next stage's job, and the reason I did not score this above the low 80s.

review.title: The loop's bound is MAX_ADVANCE_ATTEMPTS, an existing constant whose meaning is 'how many recurrence steps getNextDateAfter may take to find the next occurrence'. Reusing it here couples two unrelated limits: the new loop needs a bound on how many *skipped occurrences* to step over, and 7 is neither that number nor a safe one, as the two majors above show.
